items.q: How hard is Ukrainian for English speakers?
items.a: It takes steady work, but it's very learnable. Cyrillic usually takes a few lessons, and pronunciation is consistent — words are read the way they're written. The seven cases take the longest, so we introduce them gradually through phrases you actually use.

items.q: Do I need to know the alphabet before the first lesson?
items.a: No. We learn Cyrillic together through real words, so you're reading short phrases within the first few lessons.

items.q: I understand Ukrainian but can't speak it. Can you help?
items.a: Yes — this is very common among heritage speakers. We focus on speaking, add the grammar and spelling you missed, and gently correct the habits picked up at home, so you feel at ease with family and in Ukraine.

items.q: Can you help me prepare for the Ukrainian state language exam?
items.a: Yes. We go through the exam format and practise the kinds of tasks it includes, along with the grammar and vocabulary they require. Tell me your exam date and level in the trial lesson and I'll suggest a plan.

items.q: How often should I have lessons?
items.a: Once or twice a week works well for most people. Regularity matters more than long sessions — the five-lesson pack is an easy way to keep a steady rhythm.

seo.title: Ukrainian for Russian Speakers | Alina Zelinska
seo.description: Switch from Russian to Ukrainian calmly and without shame: surzhyk, false friends, pronunciation. Native tutor from Ukraine, 5.0 rating. Trial {{trial}}.

ufrs.title: Ukrainian for Russian speakers — *calmly, without shame.*
ufrs.lede: If you grew up speaking Russian and want to switch to Ukrainian — at work, at home or in your own head — you're not starting from zero. You already understand a lot. My Ukrainian lessons for Russian speakers help you actually speak it: naturally, correctly, and without feeling that everyone is waiting for a mistake.

sections.title: Russian helps you understand — *and trips you up when you speak.*
sections.intro: The languages are close enough to feel easy and different enough to catch you out. That's why switching needs its own plan.

items.title: You understand more than you think
items.text: Most Russian speakers understand everyday Ukrainian almost immediately. We build on that instead of starting with the alphabet.

items.title: The similar words are the hard part
items.text: Calques, false friends and surzhyk feel natural because they sound almost right. We learn to notice them — and replace them.

items.title: It's habit, not ability
items.text: Switching is about practice in a safe place. We speak Ukrainian from the first minute, at a pace that feels comfortable.

sections.title: The traps Russian speakers *fall into.*
sections.intro: These aren't signs of a poor education — they're what happens when two close languages meet. Once you see them, they're easy to fix.

items.title: Surzhyk
items.text: Russian words and endings slipping into Ukrainian sentences, often without noticing.

items.title: Calques
items.text: Phrases translated word for word from Russian that sound almost right — but aren't.

items.title: False friends
items.text: Words that exist in both languages with different meanings: «неділя» is Sunday, not a week; «час» is time, not an hour.

items.title: The vocative case
items.text: Ukrainian has a special form for addressing people, and it's the first thing native speakers notice.

items.title: Pronunciation
items.text: «и» isn't «ы», «г» is soft and breathy, «в» at the end of a word sounds close to a short «у», and «щ» is «шч». Small things that make you sound natural.

sections.title: Switch from Russian to Ukrainian *where it matters to you.*

items.title: At work
items.text: Meetings, emails, calls and presentations — we start with the vocabulary you need most often.

items.title: In the family
items.text: Speaking Ukrainian with your children or partner, reading together, answering the questions kids ask.

items.title: In your own head
items.text: Thinking, counting and texting in Ukrainian — the last step, and the one that makes the switch feel like yours.

items.title: Before an exam
items.text: If you need the state language proficiency exam, we can add exam practice to your plan.

prices.title: A sensible way *to start.*
prices.intro: Begin with a {{trialMinutes}}-minute trial for {{trial}}. For switching, the {{packLessons}}-lesson pack works well: {{packLesson}} per lesson ({{packSaving}}% off) and five focused sessions on the traps that matter most for you.

items.q: I've spoken Russian all my life. Is it too late to switch?
items.a: Not at all. You already understand most of what you hear, and that's a huge head start. What's left is speaking practice and learning to notice the Russian habits — both are very doable at any age.

items.q: I'm embarrassed to speak Ukrainian badly. Is that normal?
items.a: Completely. Many people feel that way, and that's exactly why these lessons are a calm, private space. No one is judging you here — mistakes are simply the material we work with.

items.q: What is surzhyk, and is it a problem?
items.a: Surzhyk is a mix of Ukrainian and Russian. It isn't a crime, but if you want to speak clean Ukrainian, it helps to know where it creeps in. We learn to notice it and replace it with natural Ukrainian words.

items.q: How long does switching take?
items.a: It depends on how much Ukrainian you already hear and how often you speak. The five-lesson pack is a good start: by the end you'll know your own typical mistakes and how to fix them.

items.q: Are the lessons in Ukrainian or Russian?
items.a: In Ukrainian from the start, at a pace that's comfortable for you. If a rule needs explaining, I can switch to Russian for a moment — whatever helps you move forward.

closing.title: Make Ukrainian *your own.*
closing.sub: Book a {{trialMinutes}}-minute trial for {{trial}}. We'll talk about where you want to use Ukrainian and make a calm, realistic plan.

sections.title: An English tutor who *speaks Ukrainian and Russian.*
sections.intro: Most of the lesson happens in English. But you're never lost, never embarrassed and never stuck on a rule that just won't click.

items.title: I speak your language
items.text: When a rule doesn't make sense in English, I explain it in Ukrainian or Russian in a sentence — and we get back to speaking.

items.title: I know your typical mistakes
items.text: Articles, tenses, prepositions, word order — the mistakes Ukrainian and Russian speakers make come from our own grammar. I know them from the inside.

items.title: No judgement
items.text: Many adults still carry a fear of speaking from school. Here, mistakes are part of the process: we fix them calmly and move on.

items.title: Speaking first
items.text: Every lesson is built around talking — about your work, your plans, your life — with grammar exactly where it helps you speak better.

sections.title: Where Ukrainian speakers *stumble in English.*
sections.intro: These come straight from Ukrainian and Russian grammar — which is why a teacher who knows both can untangle them faster.

items.title: Articles
items.text: Ukrainian and Russian have no «a» or «the», so they're easy to leave out — or to put everywhere.

items.title: Tenses
items.text: There's no Present Perfect in our languages, so «since» and «for» get used with the wrong tense.

items.title: Prepositions
items.text: We translate «від», «на» and «в» literally — or leave a preposition out when English needs one.

items.title: Word-for-word phrases
items.text: «Я згоден» and «я согласен» look like they need «am» — they don't.

items.title: False friends
items.text: Words that look familiar but mean something else: «магазин» isn't a magazine, «симпатичний» isn't sympathetic.

items.title: Pronunciation
items.text: th, w and v, and the short and long vowels in ship and sheep — sounds Ukrainian doesn't separate. We practise them until they stop feeling strange.

items.title: For life abroad
items.text: The doctor, the landlord, your child's school, paperwork — everyday situations where you want to feel calm, not lost.

items.title: Starting again

items.title: Before an exam

items.q: I forgot everything from school. Can I still start?

items.q: I'm afraid of speaking. What if I make mistakes?
items.a: That's the most common feeling, and it's the reason these lessons exist. Mistakes are expected and welcome — I correct them calmly and explain why, without judgement.

items.q: Can you help with English for work or moving abroad?

items.a: We can work on the skills every exam relies on — grammar, vocabulary, writing and speaking. Tell me which exam and when in the trial lesson, and I'll tell you honestly how I can help.

items.q: How often should we meet?
items.a: Twice a week is ideal if you want to start speaking soon; once a week works for steady progress. The five-lesson pack helps keep that rhythm.

writing.title: Ukrainian poetry translation *that still sounds like poetry.*
writing.lede: I'm a poet and translator working between Ukrainian, English and Russian. I translate poems, songs and books so they keep their meaning, rhythm and feeling — and I write original texts in all three languages.

items.label: languages I write and translate in: Ukrainian, English, Russian

sections.title: Literary translation, lyrics *and bilingual writing.*

items.title: Poetry translation
items.text: Ukrainian to English literary translation — and any direction between Ukrainian, English and Russian. Single poems, personal collections, work for publication.

items.title: Song lyrics
items.text: Song lyrics translation that can still be sung: rhyme, rhythm and emotional punch carried over. I also write original lyrics in all three languages.

items.title: Books and essays
items.text: Longer literary and cultural texts, translated with care for terminology, context and the author's voice.

items.title: Bilingual ghostwriting
items.text: Texts in your voice for your website, posts or personal projects — in Ukrainian, English or Russian.

sections.note: I also advise teams building Ukrainian or Russian learning apps on lesson content and learning design, drawing on 3,500+ lessons with real students.

sections.title: A book I *translated.*
sections.name: Management in Times of War
paragraphs: A Ukrainian book on leadership and management in a crisis. The job was to carry every idea — and its urgency — into clear English: precise terminology, cultural context a foreign reader can follow, and the author's voice intact.
It's the kind of work I care about most: Ukrainian voices, heard beyond the language barrier.

items.title: Read and talk
items.text: You tell me about the text, its readers and where it will live. I read it closely — meaning, images, sound.

items.title: First draft
items.text: I translate meaning and form together, so the text works as a poem or song, not just as information.

items.title: Rhythm and sound
items.text: I read it aloud and refine the rhythm and music; for lyrics, I check that every line can be sung.

items.title: Your review
items.text: We go through the translation together, and I explain my choices and revise until it feels right.

items.q: How much does a translation cost?
items.a: It depends on the length, the form and the deadline — a single poem is very different from a book. Send me the text or a sample and I'll reply with a quote.

items.q: Which languages do you work in?
items.a: Ukrainian, English and Russian, in any direction. Ukrainian is my native language, and I write poetry in all three.

items.q: Can you translate song lyrics so they can be sung?
items.a: Yes. I keep the syllable count, stresses and rhyme where possible. Sometimes the wording shifts slightly to fit the melody — I always explain those choices.

items.q: How long does it take?
items.a: It depends on the project. When I send you a quote, I'll include a realistic date.

closing.title: Have a text that needs *the right words?*
closing.sub: Tell me about your poem, song or book — the language, the length and your deadline — and I'll reply with how I'd approach it and a quote.
